messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
We need about 2,500 feet, and the flight time window is 185-195 s. Motors are limited to G or smaller. Show me what you've got.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 2,500 ft. 2500 * 0.3048 = 762 m, so the band is 762 m ±5% (about 724 to 800 m). Flight time is a hard window of 185 to 195 s, not a loose "about". Motor class is at most G. Nothing is said about rail, wind, or landing speed, so I assume a 1.5 m rail, 2 m/s wind, and a 6 m/s maximum touchdown. Single stage, straight up, sea level.
2. Feasibility: a drag-free burnout speed for 762 m is sqrt(2*9.81*762) = 122 m/s. A real model rocket gives up a large share of that to drag, so the impulse has to sit in the E to F range; a full G on a light airframe would sail well past 800 m. I need the catalog numbers before choosing.

2. Feasibility: D12 is 16.8 N*s, E12 is 27.1 N*s at 11.2 N for 2.41 s, E9 is 27.9 N*s but only 9.2 N average, F15 is 49.6 N*s, and the G80 lookup came back as a G80T at 135.6 N*s. Ratios to the E12 are 16.8 / 27.1 = 0.62, 49.6 / 27.1 = 1.83, and 135.6 / 27.1 = 5.0. The D is likely short of 724 m, the F and G are likely past 800 m on a light rocket, and the E9's lower thrust is worse off a 1.5 m rail. E12 stays inside the G cap and is the closest impulse. Its longest delay is 8 s; burn plus that delay is only about 10 s, which is early for a coast to 762 m, so the chute will be an apogee event on a plugged motor rather than motor ejection.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.12 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 11.2 / (0.12 * 9.81) = 9.5. Weight is 0.12 * 9.81 = 1.18 N, so rail acceleration is (11.2 - 1.18) / 0.12 = 83.5 m/s^2 and rail exit is sqrt(2 * 83.5 * 1.5) = 15.8 m/s, just above 15 m/s before counting the thrust spike. Propellant is about 0.036 kg, so descent mass is 0.12 - 0.036 = 0.084 kg. Time to apogee is a guess of 12 s, leaving 190 - 12 = 178 s of descent, so the sink rate for 762 m is 762 / 178 = 4.28 m/s. Canopy area at Cd 0.8 is 2 * 0.084 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4.3^2) = 0.091 m^2, and the diameter is sqrt(4 * 0.091 / 3.1416) = 0.34 m. I'll fit a 0.36 m chute so the landing sits under 6 m/s with a little margin.
4. Draft: 33.7 mm cardboard body, 0.55 m long, ogive nose, three balsa fins, 24 mm mount, Estes E12 plugged, 0.36 m ripstop chute at apogee. Checking that draft.

messages.name: simulate
messages.content: {"ok": false, "error": "invalid design: motor E12 is 24 mm but the motor_mount inner diameter is 23.8 mm"}

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: the simulate call failed before any flight numbers. The mount inner diameter is 0.0248 - 2 * 0.0005 = 0.0238 m, which is 23.8 mm, and the motor is 24 mm. Nothing else can be scored until the motor fits.
5. Fix: the failing fit is 23.8 mm against 24 mm. I'll raise the mount outer diameter from 0.0248 m to 0.0254 m and leave the 0.0005 m wall, so the inner diameter becomes 0.0254 - 2 * 0.0005 = 0.0244 m (24.4 mm). The body inner diameter is still larger than 0.0254 m, so the mount still fits the tube. Same airframe, same chute, same motor.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 501.0 m. The goal is 762 m within 5%, so 724 to 800 m, and 501.0 / 762 = 0.66, a miss. Flight time is 131.6 s against the 185 to 195 s window, also a miss. The short flight follows the low apogee: descent is about 131.6 - 8.53 = 123 s from 501 m. Gates that pass: rail exit 23.1 m/s (above 15), thrust-to-weight 9.6 (above 3), margin 2.36 cal (above 1), landing 4.0 m/s (under 6). Liftoff mass 0.119 kg matches the 0.12 kg guess. Motor is an E, inside the G limit.
5. Fix: apogee is the cause, and the flight-time miss comes with it. The F15 has 49.6 N*s against the E12's 27.1 N*s (49.6 / 27.1 = 1.83) and still sits under a G. It is a 29 mm motor, so the mount has to grow with it: outer diameter 0.0304 m, wall 0.0005 m, inner diameter 0.0304 - 2 * 0.0005 = 0.0294 m, length 0.12 m. Body, fins, and the 0.36 m chute stay put. Added motor mass is about 0.103 - 0.060 = 0.043 kg, so liftoff near 0.119 + 0.043 = 0.162 kg and thrust-to-weight near 14.5 / (0.162 * 9.81) = 9.1.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 743.6 m. Against 762 m that is (762 - 743.6) / 762 = 2.4% low, inside the 5% band, so altitude passes. Flight time 173.8 s is short of the 185 s floor by 185 - 173.8 = 11.2 s, so the window fails. Stability at rail exit is 0.86 cal, under the 1.0 cal minimum, so that gate fails too. The heavier 29 mm motor pulled the margin down. Rail exit 15.5 m/s still clears 15, thrust-to-weight is 9.1, and landing is 4.5 m/s under 6. Motor is an F, inside the G limit.
5. Fix: two misses, one cause each. Margin is 0.86 cal because the fins are small for the aft mass, so I am going from 3 fins to 4 and stretching the span from 0.055 m to 0.07 m, with the root trailing edge moved to the aft end. Flight time is the chute: descent took 173.8 - 10.4 = 163.4 s, and 190 - 10.4 = 179.6 s would land in the window. That sink rate is 743.6 / 179.6 = 4.14 m/s against the 4.5 m/s landing, so the diameter goes to 0.36 * 4.5 / 4.14 = 0.39 m. I'll fit a 0.40 m chute. Motor, body, and nose stay the same so the altitude that just passed is left alone.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 666.4 m. That is (762 - 666.4) / 762 = 12.5% under 762 m, outside the 5% band, so altitude now fails. Flight time 168.1 s is still short of 185 s by 185 - 168.1 = 16.9 s. The fin growth did what was asked of the margin: 2.13 cal at rail exit, above 1.0, and the burn stays at 2.13. Rail exit 15.9 m/s, thrust-to-weight 8.8, landing 4.2 m/s, all clear. The altitude that used to pass was 743.6 m, and 743.6 - 666.4 = 77.2 m of that went away with the extra fin area.
5. Fix: the drag of the larger fins is the new miss, so those fins go back to the set that held 743.6 m (3 fins, span 0.055 m) and the margin comes from 5 g in the nose instead. That keeps the CP where it was and shifts the CG forward, which is the 0.14 cal the earlier 0.86 cal result was short. The chute stays at 0.40 m so the descent from about 740 m can fill the 185 to 195 s window. Checking the margin of that combination before flying it.

4. Check: stability puts the static margin at 2.06 cal on a 0.169 kg liftoff, CG at 0.484 m and CP at 0.554 m. That is above the 1.0 cal launch minimum, with room for the rail-exit number to come out a bit lower than the static value. The 5 g nose weight is enough, so the design does not change. Flying it next.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 744.5 m. Against 762 m that is (762 - 744.5) / 762 = 2.3% low, inside the 5% band. Flight time 186.5 s sits in the 185 to 195 s window, 186.5 - 185 = 1.5 s above the floor. Rail exit 15.8 m/s clears 15, thrust-to-weight is 8.7, rail-exit margin is 1.3 cal (the static figure was 2.06), burn margin stays 1.3 cal, and landing is 4.2 m/s under 6. The F15 is inside the G limit. Every check passes.
5. Fix: no further change; this flight meets the altitude window, the time window, and the safety gates.
6. Uncertainty: 186.5 s is only 1.5 s inside the window, and the chute Cd of 0.8 is a model value. A real canopy that sank at 4.5 m/s instead of 4.2 m/s would scale that time to about 186.5 * 4.2 / 4.5 = 174 s and miss the floor. Rail exit at 15.8 m/s is 0.8 m/s above the gate, so a heavier build can fail the rail even if the altitude still looks fine. Drag and the 0.169 kg mass are model numbers; weigh the finished rocket.

messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Over 700 m, 38 mm mount, under 200 N-s total, site at 1,200 m elevation.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee has to clear 700 m. The motor mount is 38 mm. Total impulse stays under 200 N*s. The site is at 1,200 m elevation, so that altitude goes in every flight call. Rail, wind, and landing speed are not stated. I assume a 1.5 m rail, 2 m/s wind, and a 6 m/s touchdown. Single stage, vertical.
2. Feasibility: 700 m with no drag is sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 700) = 117 m/s, and the thin air at 1,200 m helps. An H motor is the usual fit for a 38 mm mount, but H impulse runs from about 160 N*s up past 200, so I need one that stays under the cap. Looking up a few 38 mm motors.

2. Feasibility: H123W is 235 N*s, H148R is 215 N*s, and H180W is 234 N*s and only 29 mm. H73J is 188.3 N*s, under the cap by 200 - 188.3 = 12 N*s, at 70 N, 38 mm, 0.152 m long, 0.309 kg, with a 6 s delay. That is the motor. I'll plug it and open the chute at apogee so the 6 s delay cannot end the coast early.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.50 kg. Thrust-to-weight is 70 / (0.50 * 9.81) = 14. Descent mass is about 0.50 - 0.15 = 0.35 kg. A 5 m/s sea-level landing needs 2 * 0.35 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.28 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.28 / 3.1416) = 0.60 m. Air at 1,200 m is thinner, so the same chute lands faster. I'll fit a 0.80 m chute.
4. Draft: 54 mm cardboard body, 0.70 m long, 38 mm motor in a mount with inner diameter above 38 mm, three plywood fins. The flight call sets site altitude to 1,200 m.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 1080 m, and 1080 - 700 = 380 m over the minimum. Landing is 4.4 m/s. Impulse is 188.3 N*s, under 200. Rail exit is 19.1 m/s and thrust-to-weight is 12.4. The failure is margin: 0.07 cal at rail exit and through the burn. The H73J sits far aft for these fins. Site altitude in the run was 1,200 m.
5. Fix: grow the fins. Span goes from 0.08 m to 0.13 m, root chord from 0.14 m to 0.20 m. There is 380 m of spare altitude, so the extra drag should still leave the flight over 700 m. Motor, chute, and the 1,200 m site stay.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 931.7 m, still over 700 by 931.7 - 700 = 232 m. Landing is 4.8 m/s. Impulse is 188.3 N*s. Rail exit is 18.8 m/s. Margin only rose to 0.41 cal, still under 1.0. Larger fins moved the center of pressure, but the heavy motor keeps the center of gravity too far aft.
5. Fix: add 0.08 kg at the front of the body tube. That pulls the center of gravity forward without another motor. Spare altitude is 232 m, so the extra mass should still clear 700 m. Fins, chute, and the 1,200 m site stay.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 921.8 m, over the 700 m minimum by 921.8 - 700 = 222 m. Landing is 5.1 m/s, under 6. Impulse is 188.3 N*s, under 200. Margin is 1.36 cal at rail exit and through the burn. Rail exit is 17.7 m/s and thrust-to-weight is 9.7. The motor is the 38 mm H73J. Site altitude in the run was 1,200 m. The chute opened. Every check passes.
5. Fix: no further change; the altitude minimum, the impulse cap, and the safety gates all pass.
6. Uncertainty: 222 m of spare altitude covers a somewhat heavier build than the 0.735 kg liftoff mass, but a much longer airframe would not. Margin is 1.36 cal, enough, with some weathercock in a stronger wind than the assumed 2 m/s. The 0.80 m chute is sized for thin air, and the 5.1 m/s landing moves if the canopy Cd is not the model 0.8. Rail exit at 17.7 m/s is only a little above 15 m/s.

messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Team project: The bar is 250 m; go higher if you can. No more than 20 N·s total impulse. We've got a 1 m rod to work with. We'd like the full design.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: Apogee at least 250 m, and higher is better if it still fits the other rules (minimum, with a preference to exceed it). Total impulse no more than 20 N*s (maximum). Rail is 1 m (fixed). Landing speed is not stated, so the usual 6 m/s maximum applies. Wind not stated: 2 m/s. Vertical, sea level, single stage.

2. Feasibility: 20 N*s is a D, not an E. Drag-free speed for 250 m is sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 250) = 70 m/s, so the impulse can clear the floor if the rocket is light. The 1 m rod is the hard part: average acceleration has to be high or the exit speed falls under 15 m/s. I want the D closest to 20 N*s that still has a sharp thrust curve.

2. Feasibility: D21T is 19.6 N*s, the closest of the set to the 20 N*s cap, at 22.2 N average and 32.1 N peak, 18 mm, mass 0.025 kg, delays 4 and 7 s. D12 is 16.8 N*s but only 10.4 N, weak on a 1 m rod and it leaves altitude on the table. D20W and D16 are 13.5 and 12.5 N*s. For a minimum of 250 m with a request to go higher, the D21T is the motor.

3. Size: Keep the airframe narrow so the 19.6 N*s goes into altitude. Liftoff guess 0.055 kg. Thrust-to-weight is 22.2 / (0.055 * 9.81) = 41.1. Weight is 0.055 * 9.81 = 0.540 N, rail acceleration (22.2 - 0.54) / 0.055 = 394 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 394 * 1) = 28.1 m/s. Burnout mass is about 0.045 kg. A 0.30 m chute lands that well under 6 m/s. Delay 7 s, because burnout is under a second and the coast on a light D should run several seconds past that.

4. Draft: 28 mm cardboard tube, 0.32 m long, small ogive, three balsa fins, 18 mm mount, D21T-7, 0.30 m chute. Simulated on the 1 m rail.

4. Check: The simulator gives 482.7 m, above the 250 m minimum, and it is the high side of what a D can do in this diameter, which is what "go higher if you can" asked for. Impulse is 19.6 N*s, under 20 N*s. Landing is 3.7 m/s, under 6 m/s. Rail exit on the 1 m rod is 32.8 m/s, thrust-to-weight is 39.7, margin is 1.54 cal. The chute opens at 7.9 s, just after the 7.36 s apogee, at 5.5 m/s. No warnings. Liftoff mass is 0.057 kg.

5. Fix: no change needed; the altitude floor, the impulse cap and the gates all pass.

6. Uncertainty: 482.7 m will move if the build is heavier than 0.057 kg or if the fins are thicker than the 3 mm balsa in the model. The 7 s delay is matched to this mass; more weight and it ejects early. Impulse at 19.6 N*s has little room under the 20 N*s cap if someone swaps in a hotter D. Chute Cd is 0.8. A 1 m rail exit of 32.8 m/s has plenty of margin, unlike the stability, which at 1.54 cal is fine but not generous.

Make it reach about 2,750 m in 12 m/s wind.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 2,750 m (approximate, within 5%). Wind is 12 m/s (fixed in the request). Rail, launch angle, landing speed and site altitude are not stated, so I assume a 1.5 m rail, a vertical launch, a 6 m/s landing limit and sea level. Single stage. Nothing fixes the motor or the diameter.
2. Feasibility: 12 m/s of wind is 12 / 0.447 = 26.8 mph, and the safety limit is 8.94 m/s (20 mph). The requested wind is over that limit, so the flight as written is not allowed. The closest legal case is the same altitude at 8.9 m/s. No-drag speed for 2,750 m is sqrt(2*9.81*2750) = 232 m/s, which wants a J-class motor in a slim tube. I will look up a few J and K motors for that closest version.

2. Feasibility: J350W is 669.2 N*s at 445.4 N average, a 38 mm case (0.038 m by 0.337 m, 0.651 kg) with no delay grains, so recovery has to be an altimeter at apogee. J420R is similar, 651.2 N*s, and also plugged. J800T is 1,264.4 N*s in a 54 mm case and would likely sail past 2,750 m. K550W is 1,624.9 N*s, heavier still. The J350W is the smallest of these that can plausibly reach the altitude in a 54 mm tube, and I will fly the closest legal wind, 8.9 m/s, not the requested 12 m/s.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.95 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 445.4 / (0.95 * 9.81) = 47.8. Pad weight is 0.95 * 9.81 = 9.32 N, so rail acceleration is (445.4 - 9.32) / 0.95 = 459 m/s^2 and exit speed is sqrt(2 * 459 * 1.5) = 37.1 m/s. Propellant is 0.361 kg, descent mass 0.95 - 0.361 = 0.59 kg. At 6 m/s and Cd 0.8 the canopy is 2 * 0.59 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 6^2) = 0.328 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.328 / 3.1416) = 0.65 m. I will use 0.85 m. There is no ejection charge, so the chute is set to apogee.
4. Draft: 0.14 m ogive polystyrene nose on a 0.72 m kraft-phenolic tube, outer diameter 0.054 m, wall 1 mm. Motor mount 0.042 m outside and 0.35 m long, J350W plugged. Need a hand. Get it to about 2,500 feet and keep the drift under 750 m in 12 mph wind. Use dual deployment.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: Apogee about 2,500 ft. 2500 * 0.3048 = 762 m, within 5%. Drift is a maximum of 750 m. Wind is 12 mph: 12 * 0.44704 = 5.36 m/s, and that wind has to go on every flight. Recovery is dual deployment, fixed: a drogue at apogee and a main lower down. Rail and landing speed are not stated, so 1.5 m rail and 6 m/s touchdown. The drift budget is 750 / 5.36 = 140 s of flight, roughly.
2. Feasibility: sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 762) = 122 m/s before drag. A C or D will not get a dual-deploy rocket there. I want a small G, long enough burn to not throw it all away as drag, light enough to leave the rail.

2. Feasibility: G40W is 99.0 N*s, 46.3 N average, 74.3 N peak, 2.13 s burn, 29 mm by 0.124 m, 0.123 kg. Delays exist, but dual deploy should be electronic, so the motor flies plugged. 99 N*s is about double a small F, which is the right pile for 762 m on a 41 mm rocket once drag is included. The 140 s drift budget is loose if the main opens low.
3. Size: Guess 0.28 kg. Thrust-to-weight 46.3 / (0.28 * 9.81) = 16.9, and the rail will not be close. Descent mass about 0.28 - 0.054 = 0.23 kg. A 5 m/s main needs 2 * 0.23 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.18 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.18 / 3.1416) = 0.48 m. I will use 0.65 m so landing is under 6 m/s, opening at 150 m so most of the fall is on a 0.30 m drogue. That keeps the fat chute from riding the 5.36 m/s wind for the whole descent.
4. Draft: 41 mm cardboard, wall 1 mm, tube 0.60 m, polystyrene ogive 0.16 m. Phenolic mount 0.032 m, wall 1 mm, length 0.14 m, G40W plugged. Three plywood fins, root 0.11 m, tip 0.045 m, span 0.075 m, sweep 0.05 m, 4 mm thick. A 0.04 kg altimeter. Drogue 0.30 m at apogee, main 0.65 m at 150 m. Wind 5.36 m/s on the call.

4. Check: The simulator gives 848.6 m. (848.6 - 762) / 762 = 11% high, outside the band. Drift is 533 m, under 750 m. Landing 3.7 m/s, rail exit 24.4 m/s, thrust-to-weight 14.4, margin 1.47 cal. Drogue is out at 11.0 s, which is apogee. Flight time 129.3 s. Mass 0.327 kg, heavier than my 0.28 kg guess, and it still flew high.
5. Fix: The failing value is 848.6 m. Adding nose weight has been a weak altitude lever on small rockets, and the margin has room above 1 cal, so I am adding fin area instead. Fins become root 0.13 m, tip 0.05 m, span 0.095 m, sweep 0.06 m, same 4 mm plywood. Motor, both chutes, tube, and the 5.36 m/s wind stay put.

4. Check: The simulator gives 791.2 m. (791.2 - 762) / 762 = 3.8% high, inside the 5% band. Drift is 476 m against a 750 m maximum. Landing 3.8 m/s, rail exit 24.5 m/s, thrust-to-weight 13.6, margin 1.63 cal. Drogue opens at 10.7 s, at apogee, and the flight is down in 118.6 s. Mass 0.348 kg.
5. Fix: No further fix needed.
6. Uncertainty: 791 m is near the top of the band. A cleaner fin or a lighter build will push it over 800 m, and the drag of these plywood fins is doing the work of holding it down. Drift at 5.36 m/s depends on when the main actually opens; if the 150 m setting fires late, the landing speed climbs, and if it fires early the 476 m drift grows toward the 750 m line. The 1.63 cal margin is fine in this wind but will weathercock more if the fins get larger.

I'm pretty new at this. It must stay under 850 m. I'm not high-power certified, so G or smaller. Plan for 10 km/h wind.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: Stay under 850 m. That is a ceiling. Not high-power certified, so G or smaller. Wind is 10 km/h: 10 * 1000 / 3600 = 2.78 m/s, and that goes on every run. Rail, site, and landing are not stated: 1.5 m, sea level, 6 m/s.
2. Feasibility: A G on a small tube can sit near this ceiling, so I want a G that clears the rail in 2.78 m/s of wind and still lands under 850 m. An H is out. I will look up two G motors and one F.

2. Feasibility: G40W is class G, 99.0 N*s, 46.3 N, 2.13 s, 29 mm by 0.124 m, 0.123 kg, delays 4, 7, and 10 s. G80T is 135.6 N*s, more likely to bust 850 m. F32T is 56.7 N*s and would sit well under, but a G is still legal and is the motor a new flyer would actually buy for this. On a guessed 0.25 kg rocket, thrust-to-weight is 46.3 / (0.25 * 9.81) = 18.9. A 10 s delay ejects at 2.13 + 10 = 12.1 s.
3. Size: For 0.28 kg at 4.5 m/s the chute is 2 * 0.28 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4.5^2) = 0.28 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.28 / 3.1416) = 0.60 m. I will use 0.65 m. Tube 0.041 m, mount 0.032 m, clear of the 0.029 m case. Fins a bit large so 2.78 m/s of wind does not weathercock a marginal rocket.
4. Draft: Cardboard ogive 0.14 m on a 0.55 m cardboard tube, outer diameter 0.041 m, wall 1 mm. G40W with a 10 s delay, chute at ejection. Three birch fins, root 0.10 m, tip 0.045 m, span 0.07 m, sweep 0.045 m, 3 mm. Wind 2.78 m/s.

4. Check: The simulator gives 878.6 m, over the 850 m ceiling, and the rail margin is 0.35 cal, with the burn minimum also 0.35 cal. It is over the cap because it is not flying straight, and the fins are too small. Rail exit 28.3 m/s, thrust-to-weight 19.0, and landing 3.4 m/s pass. Chute at 12.3 s, after the 10.41 s apogee, and it reached the ground. Mass 0.248 kg.
5. Fix: 878.6 m and 0.35 cal are the misses. Fins grow to root 0.14 m, tip 0.06 m, span 0.11 m, sweep 0.06 m. That pulls CP back and adds drag, which is what both failures want. Motor, tube, and the 2.78 m/s wind stay.

4. Check: Altitude is fixed. The simulator gives 773.5 m, under 850 m. The rail margin is still 0.47 cal, and the burn minimum is 0.47 cal. Bigger fins added drag and barely moved CP. Rail exit 27.2 m/s, thrust-to-weight 16.8, landing 3.7 m/s, and it reached the ground. Mass 0.282 kg. Chute at 12.3 s, after the 9.97 s apogee.
5. Fix: 0.47 cal is the remaining failure. I am adding 0.025 kg at 0.04 m from the top of the tube so the CG comes forward. Fins stay. Another fin growth would mostly buy drag. Wind stays 2.78 m/s.

4. Check: The simulator gives 781.4 m, under 850 m, and the margin is 1.15 cal at the rail and through the burn. Rail exit 25.6 m/s, thrust-to-weight 15.4, landing 3.9 m/s, chute at 12.3 s, and it reached the ground. Mass 0.307 kg. Flying straight brought the peak up a little from the last pass and it is still under the cap.
5. Fix: 781.4 m and 1.15 cal both clear, so I am leaving the nose weight in.
6. Uncertainty: 781.4 m is about 70 m under the ceiling, and 2.78 m/s of wind will move that if the nose weight is not where it was drawn. The 10 s delay opens at 12.3 s, after the 10.29 s apogee. Cd 0.8 is what makes 3.9 m/s. A real G40 in a heavier paint job still stays under 850 m; a lighter one might not.

3. Size: For 0.12 kg at 5 m/s the chute is 2 * 0.12 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.096 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.096 / 3.1416) = 0.35 m. I will use 0.36 m, just under the 5.49 m/s cap, so the chute is not a weight penalty. Nose mass 0.008 kg so the CG is not on the motor.

Landing is 4.2 m/s, under 5.49 m/s, and it reached the ground. Rail exit 23.2 m/s and thrust-to-weight 8.9 pass. Mass 0.128 kg. Chute at 10.4 s, just after the 9.28 s apogee.

1. Understand: the field ceiling is 1,500 ft maximum. 1500 * 0.3048 = 457 m, so apogee must stay at or under 457 m. Motor class at most E. Touchdown at most 15 ft/s. 15 * 0.3048 = 4.6 m/s. Rail, wind, and stage count are not stated. I assume a 1.5 m rail, 2 m/s wind, one stage, vertical, sea level. The ceiling is a maximum, so the useful design sits near it without crossing it.
2. Feasibility: drag-free speed for 457 m is sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 457) = 95 m/s. An E on a small sport rocket can reach that, and a light E rocket will go through the ceiling. I need the E-class numbers so I can pick a motor and then add enough airframe to stay under 457 m.

2. Feasibility: E12 is 27.1 N*s at 11.2 N, E9 is 27.9 N*s at only 9.2 N, and E20W is 34.7 N*s. 34.7 / 27.1 = 1.3, so the E20 is the one most likely to punch through 457 m. The E9's lower thrust is worse on a 1.5 m rail. I'll use the E12 and a wider tube than a minimum-diameter 24 mm rocket, because a slim E will clear 457 m. All three are class E, which is the cap.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.16 kg. Thrust-to-weight is 11.2 / (0.16 * 9.81) = 7.1. Rail acceleration is (11.2 - 0.16 * 9.81) / 0.16 = 60 m/s^2, so average-thrust rail exit is sqrt(2 * 60 * 1.5) = 13 m/s. The 33 N spike should clear 15 m/s. 4. Draft: 41.6 mm cardboard tube, 0.65 m long, ogive nose, three balsa fins, 24 mm mount, Estes E12 plugged. The extra diameter is what holds the flight under the ceiling.

4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 419.1 m. The ceiling is 457 m, and 457 - 419.1 = 38 m of room under it, so the maximum passes. Landing is 3.6 m/s, under 4.6. Rail exit is 22.0 m/s, thrust-to-weight is 8.4, and margin is 2.13 cal. The motor is an E12, inside the E cap. The chute opened. Every check passes.
5. Fix: no fix was needed.
6. Uncertainty: 38 m under the ceiling is enough for a normal build, but a lighter rocket than the 0.137 kg in the run will go higher and can cross 457 m. Chute Cd is a model 0.8, so the 3.6 m/s landing will move if the real canopy differs. Wind was assumed at 2 m/s. Margin is 2.13 cal, stable, with some weathercock if the wind is stronger.

messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.

For an upcoming launch: I just got my L1. My club gave me an I300. Make it fly as high as is sensible, but it must come down under 4.5 m/s. Bonus if it gets past 250 m. It has to fit in a 110 mm envelope. Provide the design and expected performance.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: the motor is an I300 (fixed). The flyer just certified L1, so the motor should stay in that class. Apogee should be as high as a sensible build allows, and clearing 250 m is a bonus minimum rather than a hard ceiling. Landing at most 4.5 m/s (maximum), tighter than the usual 6 m/s. The airframe must fit in a 110 mm envelope, so the largest outer diameter is at most 0.110 m. Wind, rail, angle and site are not stated, so I assume 2 m/s, a 1.5 m rail, vertical, sea level. Single stage.
2. Feasibility: an I-class motor in a tube under 110 mm has far more than enough impulse for 250 m. The real constraints are a stable margin, a chute slow enough for 4.5 m/s, and not building a minimum-diameter dart just to chase altitude. I need the I300's impulse, thrust, mass and delays before sizing.

2. Feasibility: the lookup returns the AeroTech I300T, class I, 436.8 N*s, average thrust 295.9 N, burn 1.47 s. The case is 0.038 m by 0.25 m and 0.4405 kg loaded, with delays of 6, 10 and 14 s. That is a legal L1 motor. Even with a heavy 54 mm airframe the bonus 250 m is easy; the 4.5 m/s landing is the number that needs a large chute. A 54 mm tube is well inside the 110 mm envelope and is a sensible L1 size, rather than a 38 mm dart.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.85 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 295.9 / (0.85 * 9.81) = 35.5. Pad weight is 0.85 * 9.81 = 8.34 N, rail acceleration (295.9 - 8.34) / 0.85 = 338 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 338 * 1.5) = 31.8 m/s on the 1.5 m rail. Propellant is 0.222 kg, so descent mass is 0.85 - 0.222 = 0.63 kg. 1. Understand: Apogee at least 2,500 m (minimum). Motor class at most M (fixed ceiling). Landing speed at most 6 m/s (maximum). Wind about 4 m/s, so the flight will be run at 4 m/s. Rail length, launch angle and site altitude are not stated: I assume a vertical 1.5 m rail at sea level. Nothing asks for staging, a payload, a duration cap or a drift limit, so this is a single-stage altitude rocket with one recovery device.

2. Feasibility: A drag-free coast to 2,500 m needs burnout speed sqrt(2*9.81*2500) = 221 m/s. Drag will eat a large fraction of that, so the airframe has to stay narrow and the motor has to be a long-burn K or L rather than a short, heavy M. An M is legal but usually lives in a 75 mm case, which costs altitude. I need impulse, average thrust and loaded mass for a few 54 mm candidates before I pick one.

2. Feasibility: The K550W is a 54 mm reload with 1,620 N*s, 536 N average thrust and a 3.02 s burn. Loaded mass is 1.49 kg, of which 0.92 kg is propellant, and the only listed delay is 0 s, so I will fly it plugged and open the chute at apogee with an altimeter. The L1000W has more impulse (2,700 N*s) but the motor alone weighs 2.19 kg in the same 54 mm diameter, and the L850W is a 75 mm, 3.67 kg case. The lighter K is the one that can actually get near 2,500 m; the bigger motors mostly haul their own casing. 3. Size: Take liftoff mass as 2.2 kg (motor plus a short phenolic airframe, fins and a small altimeter). I will use a 1.2 m ripstop chute so the landing sits under 6 m/s with a little margin. 1. Understand: two motors in a cluster (fixed count). Each motor is class D or smaller. Apogee about 95 m, so within 5%, roughly 90 to 100 m. Landing under 18 ft/s: 18 * 0.3048 = 5.49 m/s maximum. Wind, rail and site are not stated, so 2 m/s, a 1.5 m rail, vertical, sea level. Single stage. One parachute.
2. Feasibility: 95 m with no drag needs sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 95) = 43 m/s. Two D motors are about 30 N*s together, which on a light rocket overshoots 95 m, and two C motors may not lift a fat airframe at 3:1. I need both classes before I choose.

2. Feasibility: two D12 motors would be 16.8 * 2 = 33.6 N*s, about twice the impulse a 95 m flight wants. Two C6 motors are only 4.8 * 2 = 9.6 N of average thrust, so a rocket heavy enough to stay near 95 m would fall under a 3:1 thrust-to-weight. Two C11 motors are 8.8 * 2 = 17.6 N*s and 11.3 * 2 = 22.6 N, still class C, with 3, 5 and 7 s delays. That is the cluster that can both lift and stay low. They are 24 mm, so the two mounts need a tube wider than about 52 mm.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.32 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 22.6 / (0.32 * 9.81) = 7.20. Rail acceleration (22.6 - 3.14) / 0.32 = 60.8 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 60.8 * 1.5) = 13.5 m/s on average thrust. The C11 spikes to 21.7 N each, so the real exit speed should clear 15 m/s. A 0.70 m chute stays under 5.49 m/s. Burn is only 0.78 s, so a 5 s delay ejects near 6 s, about right for a short hop.

Margin is 1.89 cal at rail exit and through the burn. Landing 4.3 m/s is under 5.49. Rail exit 17.2 m/s, thrust-to-weight 6.2. Ejection at 5.8 s is after apogee at 4.47 s, so the altitude is the coast, not a premature chute.
5. Fix: 86.3 m is the miss. The 0.15 kg weight took the rocket from 172.0 m to 86.3 m, and 95 sits between them. Cutting the weight from 0.15 kg to 0.13 kg puts back 0.15 - 0.13 = 0.02 kg of the climb. Margin is 1.89 cal, so losing a little nose mass will not drop it through 1 cal. Nothing else changes.

4. Check: the simulator gives 94.9 m. Against 95 m that is 95 - 94.9 = 0.1 m, inside the 5% band. Landing is 4.1 m/s, under 5.49. Rail exit 17.4 m/s, thrust-to-weight 6.5, margin 1.77 cal at rail exit and through the burn. Two C11 motors, total impulse 17.6 N*s, both under class D. Wind is 2 m/s and the rail is 3 m, both stated, so both go on every run. Site is sea level. Drag-free speed for 2,000 m is sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 2000) = 198 m/s, which an M should beat. The sim has to actually reach the ground, so the chute cannot be so big that a high coast is still in the air at the end of the run.
2. Feasibility: I need the M1520 card before I pick a tube. An M is a lot of impulse, so 2,000 m is a floor, not the hard part. The hard part is staying stable while that much propellant burns, and still touching down under 6 m/s.

messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.

First real build here. We're an L3 team. I want to fly an AeroTech M1297. What's the highest stable rocket I can build for it? It has to land under 6 m/s. It should handle 10 mph wind. We launch off a 10 ft rail. Keep it simple if you can.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: fly an AeroTech M1297 (fixed motor). The team is L3, so an M-class motor is the right class. They want the highest altitude that stays stable, which I read as maximizing apogee while holding at least 1 cal of margin. Landing at most 6 m/s (maximum). Wind is 10 mph = 10 * 0.447 = 4.47 m/s (fixed). Rail is 10 ft = 10 * 0.3048 = 3.05 m (fixed). Angle and field elevation are not given, so a vertical sea-level launch. They asked to keep it simple, so one stage and one chute.
2. Feasibility: an M will go very high in a tube that barely clears the case. Stability is the constraint, because that motor is heavy and long. I need its impulse, diameter, mass and whether it has an ejection delay before I size the chute and the fins.

2. Feasibility: the database lists it as the M1297W, class M, 5,413.8 N*s, average thrust 1,275 N, burn 4.24 s. Case 0.075 m by 0.665 m, loaded mass 4.637 kg, propellant 2.722 kg. The delay list is only 0 s, so there is no ejection charge and the chute must open on an altimeter at apogee. A 90 mm tube is only a little larger than the 75 mm case, which is the simple way to keep the drag down.
3. Size: I am guessing 6.0 kg at liftoff. Thrust-to-weight = 1275 / (6.0 * 9.81) = 21.7. Weight is 6.0 * 9.81 = 58.9 N, so the rail acceleration is (1275 - 58.9) / 6.0 = 203 m/s^2 and the 3.05 m rail gives sqrt(2 * 203 * 3.05) = 35.2 m/s. After the propellant is gone the descent mass is about 6.0 - 2.72 = 3.28 kg. A 5 m/s landing at Cd 0.8 needs 2 * 3.28 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 2.63 m^2, which is a diameter of sqrt(4 * 2.63 / 3.1416) = 1.83 m. I will round up to a 2.0 m canopy. Four plywood fins, fairly large, because 4.6 kg of motor in the tail will otherwise leave the CP too far forward.
4. Draft: fiberglass ogive nose 0.25 m long with a 3 mm wall, then a 1.20 m phenolic tube, 0.090 m outside diameter, 2 mm wall. Motor mount 0.080 m outside and 0.70 m long, M1297W plugged. Four fins, root 0.32 m, tip 0.12 m, span 0.20 m, sweep 0.16 m, 6 mm birch plywood. Chute 2.0 m at apogee. Flying at 4.47 m/s wind on the 3.05 m rail.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: The motor is fixed as an Estes E16. Body outer diameter is at most 25 mm, which is 0.025 m. Touchdown speed is a maximum of 4.5 m/s. Apogee, flight time, rail length, wind, and launch angle are not given, so I assume one stage, the usual 1.5 m rail, 2 m/s wind, a vertical launch, and sea level.
2. Feasibility: A 25 mm tube is barely wider than a 24 mm motor case, so the E16's diameter decides whether it fits at all. I need its impulse, thrust, length, mass, and delays before sizing the airframe or the chute.

2. Feasibility: The E16 case is 0.029 m across, 0.114 m long, with 33.6 N*s, 17.3 N average thrust, a loaded mass of 0.082 kg and a 1.94 s burn. Delays on the shelf are 0, 4, 6 and 8 s. The body ceiling is 0.025 m. (0.029 - 0.025) * 1000 = 4 mm, so the bare case already sticks out past the limit. A mount wall and a body wall would add still more. No tube of 25 mm or less can swallow this motor. The request is not feasible. What fails is the body diameter against the E16 case. The 4.5 m/s landing cap never gets a chance to matter.
3. Size: There is no legal airframe to size. The nearest build that could actually fly would open the tube to about 32 mm so the 29 mm case, a thin mount and a cardboard wall all fit, then hang a chute sized for under 4.5 m/s. That build breaks the diameter rule, so I am not submitting it.
4. Check: Nothing to fly. The diameter comparison already rules the rocket out, and running a trajectory cannot shrink the motor case.
5. Fix: No change inside both constraints repairs this. A 24 mm or 18 mm motor would fit the tube, or the tube would have to grow past 29 mm. Either choice drops one of the two requirements.
6. Uncertainty: The database figure is the case diameter, not a mount outer diameter, so the real packaging gap is wider than those 4 mm, not narrower. Shop tolerance will not close a miss that large.

Need a hand. It must stay under 750 m. Keep it to an H or below. Plan for 6 m/s wind. Any ideas?

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: Ceiling, not a target. Apogee must stay under 750 m. Motor class H or smaller. Wind is 6 m/s, so that goes in every simulation. Rail, angle and site are not stated: 1.5 m vertical rail, sea level. Landing is not stated, so the 6 m/s gate applies. No diameter, no flight-time window. "Any ideas" means a practical single-stage rocket that clears the gates with margin under the ceiling, not a rocket tuned to kiss 750 m.

2. Feasibility: 750 m is an easy ceiling for H and G motors if the airframe is not tiny. Drag-free speed for 750 m would be sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 750) = 121 m/s, but I want to land well below that, so a mid-size tube and a G-class motor is the conservative choice. Checking two candidates under H.

2. Feasibility: The G64W is 118 N*s and 60.9 N average, 29 mm, mass 0.151 kg, delays 4, 8 and 10 s. That is class G, under the H ceiling. The H128W is 178 N*s and would be the one that crowds 750 m, so I leave it. Drag-free speed at the ceiling is sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 750) = 121 m/s. I am not trying to get there.

3. Size: 54 mm cardboard, long enough for a 0.14 m mount. Liftoff guess 0.30 kg. Thrust-to-weight is 60.9 / (0.30 * 9.81) = 20.7. Weight is 0.30 * 9.81 = 2.94 N, rail acceleration (60.9 - 2.94) / 0.30 = 193 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 193 * 1.5) = 24.1 m/s. Chute sizing for about 0.24 kg at 5 m/s: area 2 * 0.24 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 25) = 0.192 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.192 / pi) = 0.50 m. I will fly 0.70 m so the landing stays under 6 m/s in 6 m/s wind. Delay 8 s, ejection deploy.

4. Draft: 54 mm tube 0.55 m, ogive nose, four plywood fins, AeroTech G64W with an 8 s delay, 0.70 m chute. Wind 6 m/s, 1.5 m rail.

4. Check: The simulator gives 739.3 m, under the 750 m ceiling, with 10.7 m to spare. That is not the problem. Margin is 0.69 cal at rail exit and through the burn, under 1.0. Landing is 4.2 m/s, under 6 m/s. Rail exit is 28.1 m/s, thrust-to-weight 15.7. Impulse is 118 N*s, class G, inside H or below. The chute opened at 10.4 s, just after apogee at 10.05 s. Wind in the run is 6 m/s. Drift is 970 m, and the prompt did not cap drift.

5. Fix: The failing value is margin 0.69 cal. One change: larger fins, span 0.13 m and root 0.18 m. Extra fin drag should also pull the apogee further under 750 m, which is the direction the ceiling wants. Motor, tube and chute stay.

1. Understand: motor class is a maximum of G, because the flyer is not certified. Apogee asked is 30,000 ft. 30000 * 0.3048 = 9144 m, and the wording is a target to reach, so I treat it as a minimum. Landing limit is not stated, so 6 m/s. Single stage assumed. Rail 1.5 m, wind 2 m/s, vertical, sea level.
2. Feasibility: 9144 m with no drag needs sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 9144) = 424 m/s. A G motor tops out near 160 N*s. On a very light rocket that impulse can produce that speed only if drag is ignored, and a real 29 mm airframe at a few hundred metres per second will not. I want the largest G in the catalog before I decide it cannot be done.

2. Feasibility: G80T is class G, 135.6 N*s, 80.6 N, burn 1.68 s, 29 mm, loaded mass only 0.129 kg. G75J has more impulse, 157.4 N*s, but it weighs 0.236 kg, so the extra impulse is eaten by the motor. G125T is 124.8 N*s. HP-G138T came back as class H, which a non-certified flyer cannot use. G80T is the best legal motor. Even then, drag on a 29 mm nose at a few hundred metres per second will cap the coast far below 9144 m. I will fly the lightest stable airframe and see how short it falls.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.22 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 80.6 / (0.22 * 9.81) = 37.3. Rail acceleration (80.6 - 2.16) / 0.22 = 357 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 357 * 1.5) = 32.7 m/s. A 0.45 m chute covers the 6 m/s limit. The longest G80T delay is 10 s, and a high coast is longer than that, so the motor is plugged and the chute opens at apogee. That is the closest this class can get.

5. Fix: -0.15 cal is still the failure, and fin area is the wrong knob. Adding 0.06 kg of nose weight at the top of the tube. That is 0.06 / 0.205 = 0.293 of liftoff mass, placed ahead of the motor, which is what a negative margin needs. The G80T and the chute stay. This cannot create the missing 8 km of altitude.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: Apogee around 1,500 ft. 1500 * 0.3048 = 457 m, approximate, within 5%. Total flight time between 115 and 125 s (a range, not a one-sided cap). No motor, diameter, wind or landing speed is given. I assume a 1.5 m vertical rail, 2 m/s wind, sea level, and the usual 6 m/s landing limit. Single stage.

2. Feasibility: Drag-free speed for 457 m is sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 457) = 95 m/s. A C in a light rocket often stalls below that, and an E will usually go well past it, so a D is the class to check. Flight time near 120 s from this altitude means a sink rate around 457 / 112 = 4.1 m/s once the few seconds to apogee are set aside, which a chute can do. Looking up the D and near-D motors.

2. Feasibility: The D12 is 16.8 N*s, 10.4 N average, 1.61 s burn, 24 mm, mass 0.043 kg, delays up to 7 s. The C11 is only 8.8 N*s, the same impulse class as a C6, which is light for 457 m. The E12 is 27.1 N*s and would need a heavy airframe to stay near 1,500 ft. The D9W is close to the D12 but a reload with less propellant mass. A D12-7 in a 42 mm sport rocket is the draft.

3. Size: Liftoff mass guess 0.12 kg. Thrust-to-weight is 10.4 / (0.12 * 9.81) = 8.83. Weight is 0.12 * 9.81 = 1.18 N, rail acceleration (10.4 - 1.18) / 0.12 = 76.8 m/s^2, rail exit sqrt(2 * 76.8 * 1.5) = 15.2 m/s on average thrust. The D12 spike above that average should clear 15 m/s. Burnout mass is 0.12 - 0.021 = 0.099 kg. For a 4.1 m/s sink, canopy area is 2 * 0.099 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4.1^2) = 0.118 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.118 / 3.1416) = 0.388 m. I will use 0.39 m. A 7 s delay puts ejection near 9 s, which is about when a flight this high should top out.

4. Draft: 42 mm cardboard tube, 0.40 m long, short polystyrene ogive, three balsa fins, 24 mm mount and a D12-7. Default rail and 2 m/s wind.

4. Check: The simulator gives 327.3 m, short of 457 m. (457 - 327.3) / 457 = 28% low, outside the 5% band. Flight time is 89.5 s, under the 115 s floor of the 115 to 125 s window. That short duration is mostly the low apogee: landing is already 3.9 m/s, and there is less sky to fall through. Stability passes at 1.13 cal, rail exit 22.9 m/s, thrust-to-weight 9.4, landing under 6 m/s. Ejection at 8.7 s is a little after the 7.32 s apogee. Liftoff mass is 0.113 kg, close to the 0.12 kg guess, so the miss is drag from the 42 mm tube.

5. Fix: The failing values are apogee 327.3 m and flight time 89.5 s. One change: slim the airframe from 42 mm to 34 mm, wall 0.8 mm, and match the nose. Frontal area falls to (0.034 / 0.042)^2 = 0.655. Motor, fins and the 0.39 m chute stay. A lighter, narrower rocket should climb higher and, at a similar sink rate, spend longer in the air.

4. Check: The simulator gives 380.8 m, still short of 457 m. (457 - 380.8) / 457 = 17% low. Flight time is 114.8 s, just under the 115 s lower bound. Margin 1.53 cal, rail exit 24.3 m/s, thrust-to-weight 11.2 and landing 3.5 m/s all pass. The narrower tube helped, and it is not enough.

5. Fix: Failing values are apogee 380.8 m and flight time 114.8 s. One change: take the tube and nose down to 29 mm with a 1 mm wall, which still clears the 0.0265 m motor mount. Area scales as (0.029 / 0.034)^2 = 0.727. Fins, D12-7 and the 0.39 m chute stay. Higher apogee should also push the duration up through 115 s; if it then runs past 125 s I will shrink the chute next.

5. Fix: The 29 mm D12 cannot serve both windows at once. Apogee is 415.5 m, still under 457 m, while flight time is already 127.3 s, over the 125 s cap, because the 0.39 m chute sinks at only 3.4 m/s. Raising this airframe further would make the clock worse. The E12 has 27.1 N*s against the D12's 16.8 N*s. On the earlier 42 mm D12 flight the apogee was 327.3 m; 27.1 / 16.8 = 1.61 times the impulse, with a heavier motor, should land that fatter tube near 457 m instead of pushing the 29 mm rocket well past it. Last revision, taken together because the two misses pull opposite ways: back to a 42 mm tube, E12-8, mount lengthened to 0.10 m so the 0.095 m case fits, chute opened from 0.39 m to 0.42 m, and the fins enlarged slightly (span 0.065 m) so the heavier motor does not sink the 1.13 cal the 42 mm D12 had.

4. Check: Apogee is in the band. The simulator gives 453.7 m against about 457 m, and (457 - 453.7) / 457 = 0.7%, inside 5%. Two things still fail. Margin is 0.99 cal, under the 1.0 cal floor. Flight time is 125.6 s, over the 125 s cap by a fraction of a second. Rail exit 22.4 m/s, thrust-to-weight 8.6 and landing 3.7 m/s pass. The 8 s delay opens at 10.4 s, after the 8.37 s apogee.

5. Fix: Failing values are the 0.99 cal margin and the 125.6 s flight. This is a fourth tweak, past the usual three, because both misses are tiny and they need different parts. Fin span goes from 0.065 m to 0.075 m so the CP moves back, and the chute goes from 0.42 m to 0.40 m so the sink rate rises a little. The motor and tube stay. Apogee has room inside the 5% band if the extra fin costs a few metres.

4. Check: The simulator gives 438.9 m. The 5% floor under 457 m is 457 * 0.95 = 434 m, and 438.9 m is above it. (457 - 438.9) / 457 = 4%, inside the band. Flight time is 115.0 s, on the lower edge of 115 to 125 s but not under it. Margin is 1.07 cal, over 1.0. Rail exit 22.3 m/s, thrust-to-weight 8.5 and landing 4.0 m/s pass. The chute opens at 10.4 s.

5. Fix: no further change; altitude, duration and the gates all pass.

6. Uncertainty: 438.9 m and 115.0 s are both near an edge, so a slightly heavier build or a chute that does not match Cd 0.8 will walk one of them out. Margin is only 1.07 cal, and the heavier E12 is what put the CG back there. Deployment speed is 17.9 m/s, which the sim did not flag, but a thin plastic chute may not like it. Drag is still a model value at Mach 0.37.

1. Understand: About 450 m means 428 to 473 m. One chute. It has to land within 800 m of the pad, and the wind is 5 m/s, so that wind goes on every run. Rail, site, and landing speed are not stated: 1.5 m, sea level, and 6 m/s. Drift is the horizontal miss, not the touchdown speed. A 450 m fall at 5 m/s takes 450 / 5 = 90 s, and 90 * 5 = 450 m of drift if the wind just carried it the whole way, so 800 m is roomy if the chute is not huge.
2. Feasibility: A D has been short of 450 m once it is stable. An E is the class to try. The wind is strong enough that an overstable fin set will weathercock and walk off downrange.

2. Feasibility: Estes E12 is class E, 27.1 N*s, 11.2 N, 2.41 s, 24 mm by 0.095 m, 0.0599 kg, delays 0, 4, 6, and 8 s. The E16 is 33.6 N*s in a 29 mm case and heavier, 0.082 kg. The D12 is 16.8 N*s, light for 450 m once the fins are honest. I will fly the E12. On a guessed 0.16 kg rocket, thrust-to-weight is 11.2 / (0.16 * 9.81) = 7.1. An 8 s delay ejects at 2.41 + 8 = 10.4 s.
3. Size: For 0.16 kg at 5 m/s the chute is 2 * 0.16 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.13 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.13 / 3.1416) = 0.41 m. I will use 0.42 m so the landing stays near 5 m/s and the hang time stays short in 5 m/s of wind. A little nose mass, 0.012 kg, keeps the E from sitting on the tail.
4. Draft: Cardboard ogive 0.12 m on a 0.50 m cardboard tube, outer diameter 0.038 m, wall 1 mm. E12 with an 8 s delay, chute at ejection. Three birch fins, root 0.09 m, tip 0.04 m, span 0.06 m, sweep 0.04 m, 3 mm. Wind 5 m/s.

4. Check: The simulator gives 438.8 m, inside 5% of 450 m. Drift is 434 m, inside 800 m. Landing 4.3 m/s, and it reached the ground. Rail exit 20.6 m/s and thrust-to-weight 7.0 pass. The rail margin is 0.58 cal, and the burn minimum is 0.58 cal, so it is still short of 1 cal in 5 m/s of wind. Mass 0.163 kg. Chute at 10.4 s, after the 8.79 s apogee.
5. Fix: 0.58 cal is the miss. Altitude and drift are already good, so I am not growing the fins. I am adding 0.010 kg at 0.03 m, on top of the 0.012 kg already there, to move the CG forward with less drag than a bigger fin. Wind stays 5 m/s.

4. Check: The simulator gives 427.7 m, still within 5% of 450 m. Drift is 393 m, inside 800 m. Margin is 1.02 cal at the rail and through the burn. Rail exit 20.6 m/s, thrust-to-weight 6.6, landing 4.5 m/s, chute at 10.4 s, and it reached the ground. Mass 0.173 kg.
5. Fix: 427.7 m, 393 m of drift, and 1.02 cal all clear, so I am leaving the nose weight where it is.
6. Uncertainty: 427.7 m and 1.02 cal are both close to the line. Another 5 g in the nose, or a fin that is a little smaller, could drop one of them under. Five m/s of wind is doing real work: the drift is 393 m, and a longer hang time would use up the 800 m budget. The 8 s delay opens at 10.4 s, after the 8.85 s apogee. Cd 0.8 is what makes 4.5 m/s.

I'm new to rocketry. Landing speed below 5.5 m/s, please. I want to beat 400 m. We launch off a 2 m rail. Explain what you pick, please.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee at least 400 m, and "beat 400 m" means a minimum, not a target to trim. Landing below 5.5 m/s (maximum), tighter than the usual 6 m/s. The rail is 2 m (fixed). Wind, angle and site are not stated, so 2 m/s, vertical, sea level. The flyer is new, so a single-stage sport rocket with one chute. No motor is specified.
2. Feasibility: no-drag speed for 400 m is sqrt(2*9.81*400) = 89 m/s. A C6 in a small tube often finishes around 300 to 400 m, so it is marginal. A D has about twice the impulse and is the usual first motor that clears 400 m with room. A 2 m rail is long, so even a modest average thrust still leaves the rod fast. I will look up a D and an E.

2. Feasibility: the Estes D12 is 16.8 N*s at 10.4 N average, a 24 mm case, 0.07 m long, 0.0426 kg, with 0, 3, 5 and 7 s delays. The E12 is 27.1 N*s in the same 24 mm diameter and would fly higher than a first rocket needs. The D12 is the one I would hand a new flyer: enough impulse to beat 400 m, and the 5 s delay matches a flight of this size. The E stays on the shelf.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.12 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 10.4 / (0.12 * 9.81) = 8.83. Pad weight 0.12 * 9.81 = 1.18 N, rail acceleration (10.4 - 1.18) / 0.12 = 76.8 m/s^2, and the 2 m rail gives sqrt(2 * 76.8 * 2) = 17.5 m/s on the average thrust. The D12 spike should clear 15 m/s. Propellant is 0.021 kg, descent mass 0.12 - 0.021 = 0.099 kg. For 4.5 m/s, under the 5.5 m/s cap, area = 2 * 0.099 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4.5^2) = 0.0979 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.0979 / 3.1416) = 0.35 m. I will use 0.45 m so a heavier build still lands slowly.
4. Draft: 0.10 m ogive polystyrene nose on a 0.40 m cardboard tube, outer diameter 0.041 m, wall 0.8 mm. Mount 0.027 m outside, 0.08 m long, Estes D12 with a 5 s delay. Three balsa fins, root 0.070 m, tip 0.030 m, span 0.050 m, sweep 0.035 m, 3 mm thick. One 0.45 m polyethylene chute on ejection. Rail 2 m.

4. Check: the D12 did not clear 400 m, and it is not stable. The simulator gives 344.2 m, so 400 - 344.2 = 55.8 m short. Margin is 0.64 cal at rail exit and through the burn, under 1.0 cal. Landing is 3.1 m/s, under 5.5 m/s. Rail exit is 28.8 m/s on the 2 m rail, thrust-to-weight 11.0. Mass is 0.0967 kg, lighter than my 0.12 kg guess, so the miss is drag from the 41 mm tube, not weight. The chute opens at 6.7 s, just before the 6.94 s apogee.
5. Fix: two misses, 344.2 m and 0.64 cal. I am keeping the D12, because the motor is not the weak part, and slimming the tube. New tube outer diameter 0.033 m, length 0.36 m, wall 0.6 mm. Mount drops to 0.026 m outside so it still fits. Fins grow so the smaller tube stays stable: root 0.075 m, tip 0.030 m, span 0.055 m, sweep 0.040 m. Nose diameter follows the tube, 0.033 m. Chute and the 5 s delay stay.

4. Check: closer, still short on both. The simulator gives 392.9 m, and 400 - 392.9 = 7.1 m under the 400 m minimum. Margin is 0.92 cal, just under 1.0 cal. Landing 2.7 m/s, rail exit 31.2 m/s and thrust-to-weight 13.2 pass. Mass is 0.0801 kg. The 33 mm tube picked up 344.2 m to 392.9 m, so the D12 is simply a little light for a stable fin set on this rocket.
5. Fix: the failing numbers are 392.9 m and 0.92 cal. I am stepping to the Estes E12, 27.1 N*s, same 24 mm case, 6 s delay, and giving the fins a bit more span so the heavier motor does not push the margin back down. Mount length becomes 0.11 m to fit the 0.095 m case. Tube length 0.42 m. Fins: root 0.080 m, tip 0.032 m, span 0.060 m, sweep 0.042 m. Nose, chute and 0.033 m diameter stay.

4. Check: the E12 clears the altitude. The simulator gives 524.4 m, and 524.4 - 400 = 124 m over the 400 m minimum. Landing is 2.9 m/s, rail exit 30.2 m/s, thrust-to-weight 11.3. The chute opens at 8.4 s, just after the 8.32 s apogee. Margin is 0.98 cal at rail exit and through the burn, still a hair under 1.0 cal. Mass is 0.101 kg.
5. Fix: the failing value is 0.98 cal. Altitude has 124 m of spare, so a little nose mass is the small move. I am adding 0.005 kg of clay at the top of the tube and leaving the fins, the tube and the E12 alone. That should push the CG forward just enough without giving the altitude back.

4. Check: the clay did it. The simulator gives 1.38 cal at rail exit and through the burn, over the 1 cal floor. Apogee is 526.4 m, and 526.4 - 400 = 126 m over the minimum. Landing is 3.0 m/s, under 5.5 m/s. Rail exit is 29.1 m/s on the 2 m rail, thrust-to-weight 10.7. The chute opens at 8.4 s, just before the 8.48 s apogee, at 0.5 m/s. Mass is 0.106 kg.
5. Fix: no further change. Altitude, landing speed and the stability gates all pass.
6. Uncertainty: 526.4 m is well clear of 400 m, so a heavier cardboard tube or a coat of paint should still beat it. The margin is 1.38 cal with 0.005 kg of clay; leaving that clay out was 0.98 cal in the previous run, so the build needs that weight in the nose. Landing at 3.0 m/s depends on the 0.45 m chute actually opening. A 2 m/s wind was assumed.
messages.content:
Estes E12-6 in a 33 mm cardboard rocket, with 5 g of nose clay and a 0.45 m chute. A D12 on a wider tube did not reach 400 m, so this is the E.
On the 2 m rail it reaches 526.4 m, holds 1.38 cal, and lands at 3.0 m/s, under the 5.5 m/s cap.
The clay is what moved the margin over 1 cal. Leave it out and the rocket sits just under that floor.

Our team needs a rocket design. Target about 700 m; recovery matters most to me, so under 6 m/s at touchdown. A single chute is fine. Plan for 6 m/s wind.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 700 m (approximate, within 5%, so about 665 to 735 m). Landing at most 6 m/s (maximum), and the user says recovery matters most. A single chute (fixed), not dual deploy. Wind is 6 m/s (fixed). Rail, angle and site are not stated, so a 1.5 m rail, vertical, sea level. Single stage.
2. Feasibility: no-drag speed for 700 m is sqrt(2*9.81*700) = 117 m/s. A light F can get close and a small G will overshoot unless the rocket is heavier. 6 m/s of wind is under the 8.94 m/s cap, but it will weathercock, so I should not run the margin up near 3 cal. I need impulse and thrust for an F and a G before I commit.

2. Feasibility: the F15 is only 49.6 N*s and 14.5 N average, soft for 700 m. The G64W is 118 N*s and the G80T is 135.6 N*s, both likely to fly well past the 5% band in a light tube. The Estes F50 is 76.8 N*s at 55.8 N average, a 29 mm case (0.029 m by 0.098 m, 0.0836 kg) with a single 6 s delay. That impulse is the closest match, and the thrust is healthy on a 1.5 m rail.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.18 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 55.8 / (0.18 * 9.81) = 31.6. Pad weight 0.18 * 9.81 = 1.77 N, rail acceleration (55.8 - 1.77) / 0.18 = 300 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 300 * 1.5) = 30 m/s. Propellant is 0.038 kg, descent mass 0.18 - 0.038 = 0.14 kg. Recovery is the priority, so I size the chute for 4.5 m/s rather than 6: area 2 * 0.14 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4.5^2) = 0.138 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.138 / 3.1416) = 0.42 m. I will use 0.55 m. Burn is 1.37 s, so the 6 s delay ejects near 7.4 s, which may be a little early for a 700 m coast.
4. Draft: 0.12 m ogive polystyrene nose on a 0.50 m cardboard tube, outer diameter 0.041 m, wall 0.8 mm. Mount 0.032 m outside, 0.11 m long, Estes F50 with the 6 s delay. Three balsa fins, root 0.080 m, tip 0.035 m, span 0.055 m, sweep 0.040 m, 3 mm thick. One 0.55 m polyethylene chute on ejection. Wind 6 m/s.

4. Check: altitude landed in the band and the landing is slow, but the rocket is neutral. The simulator gives 695.2 m, and (700 - 695.2) / 700 = 0.7% low, inside 5%. Landing is 3.1 m/s, rail exit 37.7 m/s, thrust-to-weight 37.5. Stability is 0.0 cal at rail exit and 0.0 cal through the burn, which fails both the 1 cal launch gate and the requirement to stay above 0. The chute opens at 7.4 s, just before the 7.79 s apogee. Mass is 0.152 kg. Wind is 6 m/s. Drift is 1,307 m; the request does not cap it.
5. Fix: the failing value is 0.0 cal. The fins are too small for a 29 mm motor in a 41 mm tube. I am enlarging only the balsa fins: root 0.080 m to 0.11 m, tip 0.035 m to 0.045 m, span 0.055 m to 0.080 m, sweep 0.040 m to 0.055 m. Apogee has only a little room above the bottom of the band (695.2 m versus about 665 m), so I am not also adding nose mass.

4. Check: the bigger fins helped and they were not enough. The simulator gives 0.61 cal at rail exit and through the burn, still under 1.0 cal. Apogee fell to 635.6 m, and (700 - 635.6) / 700 = 9.2% low, outside the 5% band. Landing 3.1 m/s, rail exit 36.7 m/s and thrust-to-weight 36.4 still pass. Mass is 0.157 kg. I need the CG and CP before I add nose mass, because another fin increase will cost more of the altitude.

4. Check: on the pad the margin is already 1.1 cal. CG is 0.469 m, CP is 0.514 m, diameter 0.041 m. The flight number was lower: 0.61 cal at rail exit. So the pad reading is optimistic by about half a caliber, and the flight is what fails. Apogee is still 635.6 m.
5. Fix: flight margin 0.61 cal is under 1.0, and 635.6 m is under the band. I want the pad CG near 0.444 m so the pad margin is about 1.7 cal and the flight number still clears 1. Clay of 0.012 kg at the top of the tube, about 0.12 m from the nose tip, gives (0.157 * 0.469 + 0.012 * 0.12) / (0.157 + 0.012) = 0.444 m, and (0.514 - 0.444) / 0.041 = 1.71 cal on the pad. With that CG I can give some fin area back to recover altitude: root 0.090 m, tip 0.038 m, span 0.065 m, sweep 0.045 m, and I am shortening the tube from 0.50 m to 0.42 m. Chute and F50 stay.

4. Check: altitude is back in the band. The simulator gives 697.1 m, and (700 - 697.1) / 700 = 0.4% low. Landing 3.2 m/s, rail exit 36.1 m/s, thrust-to-weight 35.6. The margin did not follow the pad estimate: rail exit is 0.69 cal and the burn minimum is 0.69 cal, still under 1.0. Shrinking the fins moved the CP forward and ate most of the clay. Mass is 0.16 kg.
5. Fix: the failing value is 0.69 cal. Apogee can spare a little mass, since 697.1 m sits near the middle of the band and the floor is about 665 m. I am only increasing the nose clay, from 0.012 kg to 0.028 kg, at the same spot. Fins, tube and F50 stay, so the drag that just recovered the altitude stays put.

4. Check: the extra clay fixed the margin and, in this wind, the altitude went up rather than down. The simulator gives 716.7 m, and (716.7 - 700) / 700 = 2.4% high, still inside 5%. Rail-exit margin is 1.25 cal and the burn minimum is 1.25 cal. Landing is 3.4 m/s, rail exit 35.0 m/s, thrust-to-weight 32.3. The single chute opens at 7.4 s, just before the 7.85 s apogee, at 16.3 m/s. Touchdown is still slow. Wind is 6 m/s. Mass is 0.176 kg.
5. Fix: no further change. Altitude, the single chute, the landing speed and the stability gates all pass.
6. Uncertainty: 716.7 m is toward the top of the band. Less nose clay weathercocked more in the 6 m/s wind and flew lower, so a lighter build is not automatically higher. The 6 s delay opens the canopy at 16.3 m/s, which is harder on the chute than the 3.4 m/s landing suggests. Margin is 1.25 cal, with some room, but the result is sensitive to where that 0.028 kg actually sits. Drift is over a kilometre; the request did not limit it.
messages.content:
Estes F50-6 in a 41 mm cardboard rocket with 0.028 kg of nose clay and one 0.55 m chute.
In 6 m/s wind it reaches 716.7 m, about 2% over 700 m, leaves the rail at 35 m/s, and lands at 3.4 m/s. Margin is 1.25 cal.
The 6 s delay opens the chute at 16.3 m/s, slightly before apogee. Touchdown itself is well under 6 m/s.

Minimum apogee is 250 m. Has to land softer than 4.5 m/s. Total impulse has to stay under 40 N-s. We've got a 1 m rod to work with.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: Apogee at least 250 m (minimum). Landing softer than 4.5 m/s (maximum). Total impulse under 40 N*s (maximum, strict). Rail is 1 m (fixed). Wind and launch angle are not stated: I assume 2 m/s wind, vertical, sea level. Single stage. A 1 m rod is short, so the motor has to be punchy as well as under 40 N*s.

2. Feasibility: Drag-free speed for 250 m is sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 250) = 70 m/s, so a D or a small E is enough impulse. Off a 1 m rail, 15 m/s needs an average acceleration near 15^2 / (2 * 1) = 112 m/s^2 before gravity is even added, which points at a high-thrust D or E rather than a long-burn. Looking those up.

2. Feasibility: E30 is 33.6 N*s, under the 40 N*s cap, with 34.9 N average and a 49 N peak in 0.96 s. D12 is only 10.4 N and will struggle to reach 15 m/s on a 1 m rod. E12 is 27.1 N*s but only 11.2 N average, same problem. E20W is 34.7 N*s at 22 N, legal but softer off the rod than the E30. D21T is 19.6 N*s, which may not clear 250 m once the rocket has any size. E30-7 is the one that satisfies both the impulse cap and the short rod.

3. Size: Liftoff guess 0.09 kg. Thrust-to-weight is 34.9 / (0.09 * 9.81) = 39.5. Weight is 0.09 * 9.81 = 0.883 N, rail acceleration (34.9 - 0.88) / 0.09 = 378 m/s^2, rail exit sqrt(2 * 378 * 1) = 27.5 m/s. Burnout mass is about 0.09 - 0.018 = 0.072 kg. For a 4 m/s sink, under the 4.5 m/s cap, a 0.40 m chute is enough. Delay 7 s: burnout is under 1 s, and a flight past 250 m should still be coasting at 8 s.

4. Draft: 34 mm cardboard, 0.35 m tube, short ogive, three balsa fins, 24 mm mount, E30-7, 0.40 m chute on ejection. Rail length 1 m, wind left at the 2 m/s default.

4. Check: The simulator gives 583.6 m, well above the 250 m minimum. Total impulse is 33.6 N*s, under 40 N*s. Landing is 3.6 m/s, softer than 4.5 m/s. Rail exit on the 1 m rod is 30.3 m/s, thrust-to-weight is 35.6, and margin is 1.03 cal at rail exit and through the burn. The chute opens at 8.0 s, just before the 8.21 s apogee, at 2.8 m/s. No warnings. Liftoff mass is 0.1 kg, close to the 0.09 kg guess.

5. Fix: no change needed; the minimum altitude, the impulse cap and the gates all pass.

6. Uncertainty: Margin is only 1.03 cal, so a heavier nose or a fin that comes out smaller will go unstable before the altitude becomes a problem. 583.6 m is far above 250 m, and that extra height is sensitive to drag and to the real mass around 0.1 kg. The 7 s delay is matched to this light build; a heavier one will still be climbing at ejection. Chute Cd is 0.8. Landing at 3.6 m/s has some room under 4.5 m/s, but not if the canopy is smaller than 0.40 m.

Quick one: It needs to break 1,400 ft. It has to stay mid-power, G max. Plan for 5 mph wind.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: Break 1,400 ft is a floor. 1400 * 0.3048 = 427 m. Mid-power, G max, so nothing above a G. Wind is 5 mph: 5 * 0.44704 = 2.24 m/s, and that goes on every run. Rail, site, and landing are not stated: 1.5 m, sea level, 6 m/s.
2. Feasibility: 427 m is comfortable for a G and possible for an F. I will look up a G and use it if the card is legal, with fins and a little nose mass so it stays over 1 cal in 2.24 m/s of wind.

2. Feasibility: G40W is class G, 99.0 N*s, 46.3 N, 2.13 s, 29 mm by 0.124 m, 0.123 kg, delays 4, 7, and 10 s. G80T is 135.6 N*s, more than 427 m needs. On a guessed 0.28 kg rocket, thrust-to-weight is 46.3 / (0.28 * 9.81) = 16.9. A 10 s delay ejects at 2.13 + 10 = 12.1 s. A G in a light tube has been short of 1 cal until there is nose mass, so I will put some in from the start.
3. Size: For 0.30 kg at 5 m/s the chute is 2 * 0.30 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.24 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.24 / 3.1416) = 0.55 m. I will use 0.60 m. Tube 0.041 m, mount 0.032 m.
4. Draft: Cardboard ogive 0.14 m on a 0.55 m cardboard tube, outer diameter 0.041 m, wall 1 mm. G40W with a 10 s delay. Nose mass 0.02 kg at 0.04 m. Three birch fins, root 0.12 m, tip 0.05 m, span 0.09 m, sweep 0.05 m, 3 mm. Wind 2.24 m/s.

4. Check: The simulator gives 833.5 m, over the 427 m floor. Margin 1.09 cal at the rail and through the burn. Rail exit 27.4 m/s, thrust-to-weight 16.9, landing 4.0 m/s, chute at 12.3 s, and it reached the ground. Mass 0.279 kg. The motor is a G.
5. Fix: 833.5 m clears the floor and the gates pass, so this is the rocket.
6. Uncertainty: 1.09 cal is a thin reserve in 2.24 m/s of wind. If the 0.02 kg nose mass sits farther forward than drawn, the margin goes up and the altitude comes down, and 833.5 m still has room over 427 m. The 10 s delay opens at 12.3 s, after the 10.42 s apogee. Cd 0.8 is what makes 4.0 m/s.
messages.content:
AeroTech G40W-10 in a 41 mm cardboard airframe, wind 2.24 m/s.

2. Feasibility: the E12 is only 27.1 N*s, light for a dual-deploy bay. The F15 is 49.6 N*s but only 14.5 N average, which is soft off a 1.5 m rail. Burnout mass is 1.9 - 0.83 = 1.07 kg. A 5 m/s descent needs 2 * 1.07 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.857 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.857 / 3.1416) = 1.04 m. I will use a 1.2 m chute so touchdown stays under 6 m/s.

4. Draft: 60 mm blue tube, 0.85 m long, polystyrene ogive, four plywood fins with enough span to keep a 1.4 kg motor stable, 54 mm mount, 35 g altimeter, chute at apogee. Defaults: 1.5 m rail and 2 m/s wind.

4. Check: The simulator gives 2619.1 m. Against about 2,740 m that is (2740 - 2619.1) / 2740 = 4.4% low, inside the 5% band. Margin is 2.02 cal at rail exit and through the burn. Rail exit is 19.2 m/s, thrust-to-weight is 9.3, landing is 4.8 m/s under 6 m/s, and the chute opens at 19.3 s right at apogee. Liftoff mass is 2.13 kg, a bit over my 1.9 kg guess, which explains sitting low in the band. Peak Mach is 0.97, with no warning.

5. Fix: no change needed; altitude and the gates all pass.

6. Uncertainty: 2619.1 m is near the bottom of the 5% band, and the rocket came out heavier than I guessed. A lighter build will fly higher, a heavier one will drop out of the band. Rail exit is only 19.2 - 15 = 4.2 m/s above the gate, so the same extra mass would miss the rail before it missed the altitude by much. Chute Cd is 0.8 in the model. Drift is 812 m in a 2 m/s wind over a 531.9 s flight; nothing in the request limits that, but the recovery walk is long.
messages.content:
K185W in a 60 mm blue tube, four plywood fins, 1.2 m chute at apogee.
The simulator gives 2619.1 m, about 4% under 9,000 ft and inside the 5% band, with a 4.8 m/s landing.
Rail exit 19.2 m/s, margin 2.02 cal, thrust-to-weight 9.3.
